title: Volume of Pyramids, Cones, Spheres

findings.finding: The opening examples use square and circular base areas and recognition of a radius without an opening review.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall the base-area formulas and recognise which marked length belongs in πr² while learning the new volume rule.
findings.checked: The teaching is complete. There is no earlier topic or review; p3-definition-formula introduces the volume rule without rehearsing these area prerequisites. Diameter conversion is excluded from this finding because neither worked example uses it.
findings.assumptions: Area formulas and radius recognition are prior learning. Calculator use is assumed for numerical evaluation.

repair.proposal: Before p3-definition-text add: (a) Find the area of a square of side 6 cm. Answer: 36 cm². (b) Find the area of a square of side 9 m. Answer: 81 m². (c) A circle has centre O and a marked segment OP ending on its circumference, with OP=3 cm. Name OP and find the area to 2 d.p. Answer: radius; 28.27 cm². (d) Find the area of a circle of radius 5 mm to 2 d.p. Answer: 78.54 mm². Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse the base-area formulas and radius recognition before the worked examples.

findings.finding: The first guided cone question introduces a diameter-to-radius decision that the introductory example does not model.
findings.breakdown: Copying the example's substitution pattern with the labelled 23 mm would produce four times the correct base area.
findings.checked: p3-example-cone-item uses its labelled radius unchanged. No preceding teaching models diameter conversion. The supplied practice answer is not student-facing teaching.
findings.assumptions: Students have previously encountered radius and diameter; the issue is the additional decision in the first guided application.

repair.proposal: Before the volume working add: 'The 23 mm measurement is the diameter. First find the radius: r=23÷2=_____ mm.' Expected completion: 11.5.

findings.doneWhen: The first diameter-based guided question prompts the conversion before substitution.

findings.finding: Add a short cone sequence comparing changes in radius and perpendicular height.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes the linear effect of height and the squared effect of radius.
findings.checked: The proposed volumes are correct. The order is revised so only one dimension changes between consecutive patterned parts; the existing parts do not provide this comparison.
findings.assumptions: Students use the cone formula already taught and a calculator.

repair.proposal: After p4-q2-f, under the existing instruction, add: 'Predict how each volume compares with the first cone before calculating.' (g) r=3 m, h=4 m: 37.70 m³. (h) r=3 m, h=8 m: 75.40 m³. (i) r=6 m, h=8 m: 301.59 m³. (j) r=6 m, h=4 m: 150.80 m³. Follow with unpatterned part (k), diameter 10 m and perpendicular height 7 m: 183.26 m³. The solid type stays fixed; radius and height change in turn.

findings.doneWhen: The added parts change one dimension at a time and finish with an unpatterned application.

findings.finding: Extend the Red Pyramid question to compare doubling height with doubling the square base side.
findings.breakdown: The numerical comparison exposes the different effects of height and base area on volume.
findings.checked: The original unrounded volume is 5033600/3 m³. Doubling height gives 10067200/3 m³; doubling the base side gives 20134400/3 m³. The rounded answers and ratios are correct, using only taught methods.

repair.proposal: After p5-q5-b add: (c) A pyramid has square base side 220 m and perpendicular height 208 m. Find its volume to the nearest cubic metre. [3,355,733 m³] (d) Another pyramid has square base side 440 m and perpendicular height 104 m. Find its volume to the nearest cubic metre. [6,711,467 m³] (e) Using unrounded volumes, how many times the original volume is the volume in part c? [2] (f) Using unrounded volumes, how many times the original volume is the volume in part d? [4]

findings.doneWhen: Each follow-up part asks one question and compares the two numerical changes with the original pyramid.

findings.finding: The pyramid example substitutes 11 mm without connecting it to the labelled 22 mm base side.
findings.breakdown: Students must distinguish the full side used for base area from the half-side used in the height triangle, but that decision is unwritten.
findings.checked: p7-method supplies the Pythagoras calculation but does not explain this length selection. Earlier pyramid teaching uses supplied perpendicular heights. The diagram specification supplies no numerical 11 mm label or equality mark that directly supplies it.
findings.assumptions: Students know Pythagoras but are learning to select its lengths inside a pyramid.

repair.proposal: Before the height calculation add: 'The horizontal leg runs from the centre of the square base to the midpoint of a side, so its length is 22÷2=11 mm.'

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly derives the half-side used in Pythagoras.

findings.finding: The hemisphere example substitutes 1.75 m without showing its derivation from the labelled 3.5 m diameter.
findings.breakdown: The worked calculation leaves students to infer why the supplied length changes before it is cubed.
findings.checked: Earlier diameter-based cone practice establishes an opportunity to use the skill, but does not supply the missing connecting step in this worked example. The formula diagram identifies r as a radius.
findings.assumptions: Calculator use is assumed; selecting and deriving the radius remains a geometric decision.
findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly connects its labelled diameter to the substituted radius.

findings.finding: Follow the melted-spheres question with numerical comparisons of the resulting sphere's volume with each original volume.
findings.breakdown: The comparisons distinguish radius ratios from volume ratios in the existing context.
findings.checked: The original radius cubes sum to 216+512+1000=1728=12³. The volume ratios are 1728/216=8, 1728/512=3.375 and 1728/1000=1.728. Direct volume calculation uses taught methods.

repair.proposal: After the existing radius calculation add: (b) How many times the volume of the original sphere of radius 6 cm is the bigger sphere's volume? [8] (c) How many times the volume of the original sphere of radius 8 cm is the bigger sphere's volume? [3.375] (d) How many times the volume of the original sphere of radius 10 cm is the bigger sphere's volume? [1.728]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up compares volumes using the existing radii and resulting sphere.

findings.finding: The composite examples combine several earlier volume methods without an opening review rehearsing them.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve rectangular-prism, pyramid, cone and hemisphere formulas together while learning to combine component volumes.
findings.checked: The examples directly use these four methods. The combined-method exception requires rehearsal even though hemispheres were taught immediately before. Cylinder volume is removed from the proposed review because it occurs in guided practice rather than these worked examples.
findings.assumptions: Prism volume is prior learning from the separately taught Volume material. A calculator is available.

repair.proposal: Before p16-key-ideas-block add: (a) Find the volume of a rectangular prism 4 cm by 6 cm by 3 cm. Answer: 72 cm³. (b) Find the volume of a rectangular-based pyramid with base 4 cm by 6 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Answer: 40 cm³. (c) Find the volume of a cone of radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Answer: 15π≈47.12 cm³. (d) Find the volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm. Answer: 18π≈56.55 cm³. Ask for the formula and substitution before evaluation; keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses each component-volume method directly used by the composite examples.

findings.finding: The later practice task repeats the worked example's solid and all its dimensions without a stated retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The same rectangular prism and pyramid require the same component calculations and total; changing the requested rounding does not provide a fresh task.
findings.checked: Both supplied diagram specifications give a common 4 m by 7 m base, prism height 3 m and pyramid perpendicular height 5 m. No explicit instructional purpose for repeating these givens is supplied.
findings.assumptions: The supplied diagram specifications describe the complete mathematical givens.

repair.proposal: In p17-q1-f use a common rectangular base 3 m by 8 m, prism height 4 m and pyramid perpendicular height 6 m. Component volumes: prism 96 m³; pyramid 48 m³. Total to 1 decimal place: 144.0 m³.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains its structure but uses the replacement dimensions and answer.

findings.finding: Extend the fitted-cone question to compare the cylinder space outside the cone with the cone's volume.
findings.breakdown: This develops the central one-third relationship into a concrete remaining-volume comparison.
findings.checked: The common radius is 9 cm and height is 16 cm. Cylinder volume is 1296π cm³, cone volume is 432π cm³, and the remainder is 864π cm³, approximately 2714.34 cm³, twice the cone volume.

repair.proposal: After p20-q7 add: (b) What volume inside the cylinder lies outside the cone? Give your answer in terms of π and to 2 decimal places. [864π cm³; 2714.34 cm³] (c) How many times the cone's volume is this remaining volume? [2]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing fitted cone and asks one question per part.

findings.finding: The topic uses Pythagoras to find a shorter side without rehearsing hypotenuse recognition and subtraction.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve these decisions while interpreting unfamiliar height triangles inside solids.
findings.checked: There is no review. The preceding topic practises volumes with supplied heights. p7-method states the shorter-side formula but provides no retrieval task. Calculator evaluation of roots is excluded as a missing review piece.
findings.assumptions: Pythagoras is prior learning; a calculator is available.

repair.proposal: Before p7-method add three short items: (a) A right-angled triangle has sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm. Which is the hypotenuse? Answer: 13 cm. (b) A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 13 cm and one shorter side 5 cm. Find the other side. Answer: 12 cm. (c) A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 10 cm and one shorter side 4 cm. Write the calculation for the other side before evaluating. Answer: √(10²−4²), approximately 9.17 cm. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse identifying the hypotenuse and subtracting squares before interpreting the solid diagrams.

findings.finding: Follow the edge-height question with a pyramid using the same numerical length as a face slant height.
findings.breakdown: The comparison makes the choice between half a diagonal and half a side consequential for volume.
findings.checked: Both methods are available through p7-examples and the hint in p9-q2. Independent calculation gives volumes 2748.7371 cm³ and 3055.0505 cm³, so the proposed difference is corrected to 306.3 cm³.
findings.assumptions: Students retain unrounded intermediate values and use a calculator.

repair.proposal: After p9-q2-response add: (b) 'A second square pyramid has the same 20 cm base side, but its face slant height is 25 cm. Find its volume to 1 d.p.' Answer: h=√525 cm; V=3055.1 cm³. (c) 'By how much does the second pyramid's volume exceed the first pyramid's volume? Answer to 1 d.p.' Answer: 306.3 cm³, using unrounded values.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up compares the two height interpretations using the corrected volume difference.

findings.finding: Extend the doubled-radius question with inverse volume comparisons.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the cubic radius relationship with recovering a radius and compensating for a hemisphere's half-volume factor.
findings.checked: For part (b), the radius is 6 cm. For part (c), equating the hemisphere volume to the original sphere gives r³=54, hence r≈3.78 cm. The tasks use the taught formulas and prior equation-solving methods.
findings.assumptions: Students can rearrange numerical formulas and evaluate cube roots, covered separately in the course library.

repair.proposal: After the existing question, treated as part (a), add: (b) 'A ball has radius 3 cm. Another ball has eight times its volume. What is the other ball's radius?' Answer: 6 cm. (c) 'A hemisphere has the same volume as the original ball of radius 3 cm. Find the hemisphere's radius to 2 d.p.' Answer: ∛54≈3.78 cm.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up parts are attached to p13-q8 and include their expected answers.

findings.finding: Extend the water-cone question with a sequence varying the water's linear scale.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes how proportional changes in depth and surface radius produce cubic changes in the filled fraction.
findings.checked: All dimensions are consistent with similar cones and all proposed fractions are correct. The repeated half-depth case has an explicit comparison purpose within the prediction sequence. Students can calculate every fraction using the taught cone formula.
findings.assumptions: The added parts retain the existing inverted-cone context, with depths measured from the apex.

repair.proposal: After p19-q4-b add: 'Predict each fraction before calculating.' (c) 'In the same cone, water has depth 3 cm and surface radius 2 cm. What fraction is filled?' Answer: 1/64. (d) 'Water has depth 6 cm and surface radius 4 cm. What fraction is filled?' Answer: 1/8. (e) 'Water has depth 9 cm and surface radius 6 cm. What fraction is filled?' Answer: 27/64. (f) 'Water has depth 12 cm and surface radius 8 cm. What fraction is filled?' Answer: 1. Follow with unpatterned part (g): 'A different cone has height 15 cm and radius 10 cm; water has depth 6 cm and surface radius 4 cm. What fraction is filled?' Answer: 8/125. The patterned run keeps the full cone fixed and varies the water's scale.

findings.doneWhen: The prediction sequence follows the existing question and ends with an unpatterned application.

contextQuestions.question: Have students already learned to calculate a volume percentage when no dimensions are supplied, by choosing convenient dimensions or using algebraic dimensions? This determines whether these questions require a cue introducing that approach.

protectedGroups.observation: The sequence isolates radius givens, then diameter givens, before requiring students to distinguish them in a mixed set.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the given length is a radius or diameter, and how a diameter is represented.

protectedGroups.observation: Hemisphere practice moves from a marked radius to diameters and then changes orientation, reinforcing that orientation does not change the formula.
protectedGroups.varies: Given radius versus diameter, and bowl versus dome orientation.
protectedGroups.invariant: Volume is half the volume of a sphere of the same radius.

protectedGroups.observation: The same volume formula applies when base area and perpendicular height are supplied, despite changes in solid and orientation.
protectedGroups.varies: Base shape, orientation, dimensions and units.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base area is given directly; each calculation is V=Ah/3.

protectedGroups.observation: Rotating a cone does not change which perpendicular distance serves as its height.
protectedGroups.invariant: A radius and perpendicular height are supplied, with their right-angle relationship marked.

protectedGroups.observation: A second hemispherical end changes the component count while retaining the cylinder-and-rounded-end structure.
protectedGroups.varies: One hemispherical end becomes two; dimensions also change.
protectedGroups.invariant: Horizontal cylindrical middle with a common circular cross-section.

protectedGroups.observation: The same fitted sphere occupies different proportions of two enclosing solids.
protectedGroups.varies: The enclosing solid changes from cube to cylinder.
protectedGroups.invariant: The sphere fits exactly and the task asks for its percentage of the container volume.

dropped.reason: The mathematics is correct and the instruction meets the one-line prediction rule, but only four suggestions may be retained. The existing p19-q4 already explicitly contrasts height fraction with volume fraction; the four retained suggestions provide stronger additional opportunities across the booklet.

candidates.finding: Vary the water depth in the same cone to expose the relationship between height fraction and volume fraction.

droppedQuestions.question: Before this booklet, have students learnt to solve equations such as (4π/3)r³ = 15 by dividing by the whole coefficient and then taking a cube root, for example in Simple Cubic Equations? If not, p12-q5 needs a short worked inverse-volume example before students attempt it.
droppedQuestions.reason: Solving a cubic equation by dividing by its coefficient and taking a cube root is separately taught course content, identified by Simple Cubic Equations and the equations/formulas booklets. Its absence from this volume booklet does not establish missing new teaching.

droppedQuestions.question: Have students already learned that similar solids' volume ratios are the cubes of their length ratios, and practised reversing that relationship with a cube root? The supplied earlier teaching does not show this, although the course library includes Similar Areas and Volumes and Simple Cubic Equations.
droppedQuestions.reason: The course explicitly provides Similar Areas and Volumes and Simple Cubic Equations, which cover the knowledge named. This labelled closing mastery question combines those separately taught methods; their absence from this booklet's teaching does not require a context question.
